title: Data Gathering
abstract:
Stage 2 of the MLDLC. The five sources named in the notes — CSV/Excel, JSON,
SQL, APIs and web scraping — with when each applies, the code to read from
each, the failure modes that will bite you (encodings, delimiters, nested JSON,
pagination, rate limits, brittle selectors), the legal and ethical boundaries on
scraping, and the one decision that must be made at the end of this stage:
splitting off a test set before you look at anything.

blocks.t: The Five Sources

blocks.cap:
The sources ordered left to right by how much engineering they demand.
 A CSV is a morning's work; a scraper is a system you will maintain forever.

head: Source
Used when
Reader
rows: Data is already available as files
Real-time or live data is needed
Only when no API is available

blocks.t: The ordering is a preference ranking

Always prefer the leftmost source that can supply what you need. A database
query is reproducible, typed and fast. A scraper is none of those things — it
breaks whenever somebody redesigns a page, and it may not be permitted at all.
Scraping is the option of last resort, not a first move.
CSV and Excel
The simplest case, and still the source of a remarkable number of silent bugs.

head: Problem
Symptom and fix
rows: UnicodeDecodeError, or mojibake in names. Try encoding="utf-8", then "latin-1", then "cp1252"
Everything lands in one column. Pass sep=";" or sep="\t"
Header row is garbage. Use skiprows=
"1,234" parsed as a string. Use thousands=","
An ID column of digits becomes an int and loses leading zeros. Use dtype={"id": str}
Gene names and part numbers turned into dates before you got the file — a genuinely famous problem
Use chunksize= and process incrementally (out-of-core, Topic 03)

blocks.t: JSON

Used for semi-structured data, mostly from APIs. The distinguishing property is
nesting: JSON records can contain objects and arrays, whereas a dataframe
row cannot.
Flattening is the whole job

pd.json_normalize is the tool. It turns {"user": {"id": 1,
"name": "A"}} into columns user.id and user.name. For arrays,
record_path explodes a nested list into rows while meta carries
parent fields down. Getting these two arguments right is most of the work of
consuming an API.
SQL

Used when data is stored in databases. This is the best-case source: the schema
is explicit, types are enforced, and the join happens close to the data.
Push the work into the database

Do not SELECT * a hundred-million-row table into pandas and filter there.
Filter, aggregate and join in SQL; pandas receives only the result. The database
has indexes and a query planner; pandas has neither.
Never build SQL with string formatting

f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}" is a SQL-injection hole
even in an internal script, and it breaks the moment a value contains a quote.
Use parameter binding — pass the values separately and let the driver escape
them.
APIs

Used to fetch real-time or live data. The mechanics are simple; the operational
concerns are not.

head: Concern
What to do
rows: Keys in environment variables, never in the notebook, never in git
Respect 429 and the Retry-After header; back off exponentially
Loop until the cursor or next link is exhausted; never assume one page
Always pass timeout=; a hung request will otherwise block forever
Retry on 5xx and connection errors, not on 4xx — a 400 will fail identically forever
The provider may add or rename fields without notice; validate on read
Cache raw responses to disk so a re-run does not re-hit the API

blocks.t: Web Scraping
The rule from the notes

Used only when no API is available. If the site publishes an API, use it
— it is faster, stable, permitted, and returns clean structured data.
The legal and ethical boundary

rows: Check it and honour it. It states what the site owner permits
Many explicitly prohibit automated access; violating them is a contractual issue regardless of technical feasibility
Throttle deliberately. Hammering a small site is a denial-of-service, however unintentional
GDPR/DPDP apply to scraped personal data exactly as they do to collected data
Facts are generally not copyrightable; expression is
Set an honest User-Agent with contact details

blocks.t: Why scrapers break

Selectors are tied to markup, and markup changes. A scraper is not a script you
write once — it is a system with an ongoing maintenance cost. Prefer stable
anchors (id, data- attributes, semantic tags) over brittle ones
(long CSS paths, positional nth-child). And note that much of the modern
web renders content in JavaScript, so requests returns an empty shell and
you need a headless browser.
Code

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, json, os, time

# =====================================================================
# 1. CSV / EXCEL
# =====================================================================
df = pd.read_csv(
    "data.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",          # try latin-1 / cp1252 on UnicodeDecodeError
    sep=",",                   # ";" in much of Europe, "\t" for TSV
    thousands=",",             # so "1,234" parses as 1234
    parse_dates=["signup_date"],
    dtype={"customer_id": str},   # keep leading zeros; IDs are NOT numbers
    na_values=["", "NA", "N/A", "null", "-", "?"],   # site-specific sentinels
)

# Larger than memory -> stream it (out-of-core, Topic 03)
total = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv("huge.csv", chunksize=100_000):
    total += chunk["amount"].sum()

# Excel: read every sheet at once
sheets = pd.read_excel("book.xlsx", sheet_name=None)   # dict of DataFrames
for name, sheet in sheets.items():
    print(name, sheet.shape)


# =====================================================================
# 2. JSON -- the work is FLATTENING
# =====================================================================
raw = [
    {"user": {"id": 1, "name": "Asha"}, "plan": "premium",
     "sessions": [{"d": "2026-03-01", "min": 45},
                  {"d": "2026-03-02", "min": 12}]},
    {"user": {"id": 2, "name": "Bilal"}, "plan": "basic",
     "sessions": [{"d": "2026-03-01", "min": 8}]},
]

flat = pd.json_normalize(raw)                       # user.id, user.name, plan
print(flat.columns.tolist())

# Explode the nested list into ROWS, carrying parent fields down:
sessions = pd.json_normalize(
    raw, record_path="sessions", meta=[["user", "id"], "plan"])
print(sessions)
#            d  min  user.id     plan
# 0 2026-03-01   45        1  premium ...


# =====================================================================
# 3. SQL -- push the work into the database
# =====================================================================
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
engine = create_engine(os.environ["DB_URL"])        # never hard-code creds

# WRONG: pulls 100M rows into RAM, then filters
# df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM transactions", engine)

# RIGHT: the database filters, joins and aggregates; pandas gets the answer
query = text("""
    SELECT  u.user_id,
            u.plan,
            COUNT(t.txn_id)              AS n_txn,
            SUM(t.amount)                AS total_spend,
            MAX(t.created_at)            AS last_txn
    FROM    users u
    LEFT JOIN transactions t ON t.user_id = u.user_id
    WHERE   t.created_at >= :since        -- bound parameter, never an f-string
      AND   u.status = 'active'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.plan
""")
df = pd.read_sql(query, engine, params={"since": "2026-01-01"})

# Very large result sets: iterate instead of materialising
for chunk in pd.read_sql(query, engine, params={"since": "2020-01-01"},
                         chunksize=50_000):
    ...   # process incrementally


# =====================================================================
# 4. APIs -- retries, backoff, pagination, caching
# =====================================================================
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

def make_session() -> requests.Session:
    s = requests.Session()
    retry = Retry(
        total=5,
        backoff_factor=1.0,                  # 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s
        status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],   # retry these
        allowed_methods=["GET"],             # never blindly retry writes
    )
    s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))
    s.headers.update({
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['API_KEY']}",   # NOT in the code
        "User-Agent": "research-bot/1.0 (contact: me@example.com)",
    })
    return s

def fetch_all(url, session, page_size=100):
    """Follow pagination to exhaustion. Never assume a single page."""
    out, cursor = [], None
    while True:
        params = {"limit": page_size}
        if cursor:
            params["cursor"] = cursor
        r = session.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)   # ALWAYS set timeout
        r.raise_for_status()
        payload = r.json()
        out.extend(payload["data"])
        cursor = payload.get("next_cursor")
        if not cursor:
            return out
        time.sleep(0.2)                       # be polite even under the limit

# Cache raw responses so a re-run costs nothing:
def cached_fetch(url, session, path="cache.json"):
    if os.path.exists(path):
        return json.load(open(path))
    data = fetch_all(url, session)
    json.dump(data, open(path, "w"))
    return data


# =====================================================================
# 5. WEB SCRAPING -- last resort, and check permission first
# =====================================================================
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def may_i_scrape(url: str, agent: str = "research-bot") -> bool:
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    rp.set_url(url.rstrip("/") + "/robots.txt")
    rp.read()
    return rp.can_fetch(agent, url)

def scrape_listing(url, session):
    if not may_i_scrape(url):
        raise PermissionError("robots.txt disallows this path")

    html = session.get(url, timeout=30).text
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")

    rows = []
    for card in soup.select("[data-testid='product-card']"):   # STABLE anchor
        title = card.select_one("h3")
        price = card.select_one("[data-price]")
        rows.append({                       # defensive: any field may be absent
            "title": title.get_text(strip=True) if title else None,
            "price": price["data-price"] if price else None,
        })
        time.sleep(1.0)                      # throttle deliberately
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# Prefer:  [data-testid='product-card']     stable, semantic
# Avoid:   div.container > div:nth-child(3) > span.a4kx2   breaks on redesign
# JS-rendered pages return an empty shell to requests -> use Playwright.


# =====================================================================
# 6. THE LAST STEP OF THIS STAGE: SPLIT BEFORE YOU LOOK
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = df.drop(columns="target"), df["target"]
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
# For temporal data use a chronological cut instead -- a shuffled split
# lets the model learn from the future to predict the past.

# Persist the RAW pull so the whole pipeline is reproducible from source:
df.to_parquet("raw_2026_03_01.parquet")     # parquet keeps dtypes; CSV does not
Parquet over CSV for intermediate storage

CSV loses every dtype — dates become strings, integers become floats once a
null appears, and categories become objects. Parquet preserves the schema, is
columnar, compresses roughly $5\times$ better and reads far faster. Use CSV only
at the boundaries where a human or another system needs it.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
CSV/Excel — data already available as files. Watch encoding,
 delimiter, thousands separators, and dtype coercion on ID columns.

JSON — semi-structured, mostly from APIs. The work is
 flattening: json_normalize with record_path and
 meta.

SQL — data stored in databases. Push filtering, joining and
 aggregation into the query; use bound parameters, never f-strings.

APIs — real-time or live data. Handle auth, rate limits,
 pagination, timeouts, retries with backoff, and cache the raw responses.

Web scraping — only when no API is available. Check
 robots.txt and the terms of service, throttle, use stable
 selectors, and expect to maintain it forever.
Prefer the leftmost source that can do the job. Scraping is last resort.

Finish this stage by persisting the raw pull (Parquet) and
 splitting off a test set before you look at anything.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. When would you scrape instead of using an API?

Only when no API exists or the API does not expose the fields you need, and only
after checking robots.txt and the terms of service. Scraping is slower,
more fragile, legally riskier and higher maintenance.

Q. Your CSV of customer IDs loses leading zeros. Why, and what is the
fix?

Pandas infers the column as an integer. Pass dtype={"customer_id": str}.
The general principle: identifiers are strings, not numbers — you never do
arithmetic on them.

Q. A pandas query on a 200M-row table takes 40 minutes. What do you
change?

Do not load it into pandas. Push the filtering, joining and aggregation into SQL
so the database uses its indexes and returns only the result set. If it must be
in Python, read in chunks or use a columnar engine.
Q. The API you depend on starts returning 429. What do you do?

Respect it. Back off exponentially, honour the Retry-After header, reduce
concurrency, and cache responses so re-runs do not re-hit the endpoint. Do not
retry immediately in a tight loop — that is how keys get revoked.
Q. When should you split the data into train and test?

At the end of data gathering, before any exploration. If you explore the full
dataset and then split, your modelling decisions were informed by the test set
— leakage that no code review catches.
